# Luke 16: verse-by-verse research notes

**About these notes:** I ran out of search and fetch tools before I could finish. Several full-chapter pages (Enduring Word, the Pulpit Commentary, bible.org) cut off partway through, so I filled some verses from search snippets. I found nothing from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, oca.org, the Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org) or the Wesleyan sites (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com). I also found no page on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching about this chapter. Where a point needs one of those sources, I've left it out.

## Part 1: The shrewd manager (vv. 1–13)

**v. 1**
- Pulpit Commentary: this parable has been explained in more ways than any other. It sets aside readings that make the steward stand for the Pharisees, tax collectors, Judas or Satan, and takes the parable as a lesson for every disciple. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/16.htm
- Ellicott takes the opposite view: the Unjust Steward represents primarily the Pharisees and scribes in their teaching and ministerial functions. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/16.htm
- Coffman agrees with Ellicott. The parable was spoken to the disciples but is about Israel's religious leaders, and the rich man stands for God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/luke-16.html
- Guzik: this is a different occasion from Luke 15, though Pharisees were listening. He quotes Barclay that "The steward had followed a career of embezzlement." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-16/

**v. 2**
- Pulpit: losing the stewardship stands for death, when God takes back everything he lent us. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/16.htm
- Guzik: everyone, believer or not, will give God an account. He cites Spurgeon's list of what we answer for: our time, talents, possessions and influence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-16/

**v. 3**
- A comment on StudyLight's Luke 16:8 page says the man is not old or lame but lazy: his "cannot dig" really means "will not." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/16-8.html
- Matthew Henry: the steward had more reason to be ashamed of cheating his master than of begging. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/luke-16.html

**v. 4**
- Pulpit: the second half of the parable teaches that kindness to the poor and helpless is a sure way to prepare for death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/16.htm

**vv. 5–7**
- Pulpit: these verses just fill in the picture. Guessing why each debtor got a different reduction is not worthwhile. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/16.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB): the steward cut one debt by half and the other by a fifth. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Luk/Luk_016.cfm
- Ellicott: by making the debtors partners in the fraud, the steward bought both their goodwill and their silence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/16.htm

**v. 8**
- *The traditional reading:* the master praises the steward's foresight, not his fraud. Barnes: It is not said that his master commended him because he was "unjust," but because he was "wise." JFB and Clarke say the same. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/16-8.html and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/luke-16.html
- "The master" is the steward's employer, not Jesus. Ellicott says the master is himself a man of this world who admires sharp dealing. https://biblehub.com/luke/16-8.htm
- Pulpit calls the praise a graphic and sarcastic eulogy which a good-humoured man of the world would pronounce. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-16.html
- *A different view of the facts:* the Cambridge Bible suggests the steward's last act was in a sense honest. He billed the debtors the correct amount for the first time, while presenting the cut as a favour he had won from his lord. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/16-8.htm
- Preceptaustin quotes a similar idea, that the steward was staying within the letter of the law and acting within the authority given to him, but was still acting for himself. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-16-commentary
- Application: Guzik says worldly people pursue profit with more zeal than believers pursue the kingdom. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-16/
- Steven Cole (bible.org) says Jesus is not praising the man's crookedness, but rather his shrewdness in using a present opportunity to provide for his inevitable future needs. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-74-how-be-truly-rich-luke-161-13

**v. 9**
- Pulpit: "mammon" is an Aramaic word for money, not the name of a god.
  - "Unrighteous" is added because getting money is so often tainted.
  - Some expositors say the "friends" are angels; Pulpit thinks they are the poor we have helped, who will welcome us.
  - Older manuscripts read "when it (money) fails" rather than "when you fail."
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/16.htm
- *Merit and almsgiving (a Protestant/Catholic point):* Pulpit quotes Godet that the parable undermines the idea that giving to the poor earns merit, since the money is God's anyway. Pulpit still holds that God regards loving almsgiving when deciding our eternal destiny, citing Cornelius and 1 Timothy 6. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/16.htm
- Calvin warns those who think giving to the poor makes up for sensual living. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/luke/16.htm
- Guzik: invest your resources for eternity now, not someday. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-16/

**v. 10**
- Pulpit: this is the broad rule by which God decides a soul's future. It also limits the parable: in the end, faithfulness is what gets rewarded, not trickery. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/16.htm

**v. 11**
- Guzik: "true riches" means spiritual riches. People who handle money badly should not be trusted with spiritual leadership. That is about how well they manage, not how much they have. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-16/

**v. 12**
- JFB: Here all we have is on trust as stewards, who have an account to render. In the next life, what the faithful receive will be truly their own. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Luk/Luk_016.cfm
- Cole (on preceptaustin): "much," "true riches" and "your own" all mean treasure stored up in heaven. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-16-commentary

**v. 13**
- Guzik: a person can *have* both money and God but cannot *serve* both. A test of which one you serve is what you will sacrifice for. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-16/
- Preceptaustin: Either God owns you, including your money, or your money (mammon) owns you. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-16-commentary
- Pulpit: the rich man of vv. 19–31 is an example of trying to serve both. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/16.htm

## Part 2: Jesus answers the Pharisees (vv. 14–18)

**v. 14**
- Pulpit: the Pharisees' scorn was probably aimed at Jesus' own poverty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/16.htm
- Ellicott: they felt the force of the rebuke and covered it with mockery. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/16.htm
- Barclay (quoted by Guzik): the word means they "turned up their noses." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-16/

**v. 15**
- Deffinbaugh (bible.org): the root problem was looking for approval from the wrong judge and by the wrong standard, outward appearance.
  - Money counted for the Pharisees as visible proof of godliness, because of the promises of prosperity in Deuteronomy 28. This is the nearest thing I found to a comment on prosperity thinking, and it is about the Pharisees, not modern teaching.
  
  https://bible.org/seriespage/rich-man-and-lazarus-luke-1614-31

**v. 16**
- Deffinbaugh: an old era ended with John and a new one began, with people pushing to get into the kingdom. https://bible.org/seriespage/rich-man-and-lazarus-luke-1614-31
- *Two readings of "forcing his way in":* Guzik takes it as the zeal of eager followers. He also reports Pate's view that it describes demonic and human opposition forcing its way in, and says both may be true. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-16/

**v. 17**
- Deffinbaugh: the new era does not abolish the Old Testament; Jesus fulfils it. The Pharisees claimed to protect the Law but were in fact corrupting it. https://bible.org/seriespage/rich-man-and-lazarus-luke-1614-31

**v. 18** *(a real disagreement among Protestant teachers)*
- Deffinbaugh: this verse is an example of the Pharisees setting the Law aside. Jesus stresses the rule, not the exceptions. https://bible.org/seriespage/rich-man-and-lazarus-luke-1614-31
- John Piper (Baptist): Luke 16:18 calls all remarriage after divorce adultery. He says he moved away from the common Protestant view that allows remarriage after adultery or desertion. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/divorce-and-remarriage-a-position-paper
- The elders of Piper's own church (Bethlehem) take a wider view: if there are biblical grounds at all, they are unrepentant adultery and long-term desertion. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/what-god-has-joined-together-let-not-man-separate-part-2
- Preceptaustin: John MacArthur and D. A. Carson and the vast majority of Christendom today accept exception clauses, while Piper, Boice and Baucham do not. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-19-commentary
- A Bible Hub article reads Luke's wording as a short statement of the rule. The exceptions are recorded by Matthew (sexual immorality) and Paul (desertion by an unbeliever). https://biblehub.com/q/Luke_16_18_on_divorce_remarriage.htm

## Part 3: The rich man and Lazarus (vv. 19–31)

**v. 19**
- *Parable or true story? Teachers differ:*
  - Guzik: Jesus did not call it a parable and names a character, so it is an actual case history. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-16/
  - Calvin also leans towards a real event. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/luke/16.htm
  - Luther said the opening at least seemed to him historical. https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/wbc/t/the-rich-man-and-lazarus.html
  - MacArthur says it is purely a parable. https://www.gty.org/sermons/CONF-RC08-10/the-rich-man-and-lazarus-2008-resolved-conference
  - Deffinbaugh: a parable, but true in what it says about life after death. https://bible.org/seriespage/rich-man-and-lazarus-luke-1614-31
  - Clarke leaves the question open. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/luke-16.html
- Calvin: fine clothes and good food are not wrong in themselves, but they are rarely kept within limits. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/luke/16.htm
- Coffman: nothing suggests the man's wealth was gained dishonestly. His sin is indifference. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/luke-16.html

**v. 20**
- Lazarus means "God has helped." Cole notes the beggar is named while the rich man is not. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-16-commentary
- Carson: Lazarus was too ill to beg and had to be carried to the gate. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/the-rich-man-and-lazarus-en/

**v. 21**
- Carson: At least the dogs had a modicum of compassion when the rich man had none. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/the-rich-man-and-lazarus-en/
- Calvin's chief charge against the rich man is cruelty: he let Lazarus lie at his gate. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/luke/16.htm
- Clarke differs. He thinks the crumbs were probably given and that the text never accuses the rich man of turning Lazarus away. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/luke-16.html

**v. 22**
- Calvin: the rich man's burial is mentioned, but nothing is said of Lazarus's body. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/luke/16.htm
- Pulpit (on Bible Hub): the angels carried only the soul. Jews used "Abraham's bosom" for the home of happy but waiting souls. https://biblehub.com/luke/16-22.htm
- Constable (dispensational): Lazarus is shown enjoying the future messianic banquet in the millennial kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/16-22.html
- *Catholic view:* the Catholic Encyclopedia says the imagery comes from popular Jewish ideas of the time, in which the dead gathered in Sheol/Hades and one part was a place of rest. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01055a.htm
- Catholic tradition calls "Abraham's bosom" the *limbus patrum* (the "limbo of the fathers," where the Old Testament righteous waited). https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/09256a.htm
- Deffinbaugh (evangelical) similarly believes in an Old Testament "holding place" with two compartments. https://bible.org/seriespage/rich-man-and-lazarus-luke-1614-31

**v. 23**
- MacArthur: people in hell cannot really see people in heaven. The sight across the gulf is a storytelling device. https://www.gty.org/sermons/CONF-RC08-10/the-rich-man-and-lazarus-2008-resolved-conference
- Carson: the rich man recognised Lazarus, so he cannot claim not to have known Lazarus was at his gate. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/the-rich-man-and-lazarus-en/

**v. 24**
- JFB: calling Abraham "Father" is a real but useless claim of descent, and he asks mercy though he never showed any. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Luk/Luk_016.cfm
- Guzik: he still treats Lazarus as his servant, so death did not remove his sense of entitlement. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-16/
- Preceptaustin: he offers no apology but never complains his punishment is unfair either. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-16-commentary

**v. 25**
- Several writers say neither man's fate depended on wealth or poverty. Guzik says Lazarus must have had real faith. Cole and Stedman note that Abraham was rich, and that Lazarus believed Moses and the prophets. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-16/ and https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-16-commentary
- Coffman criticises readings that make wealth evil in itself. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/luke-16.html
- *Older critical scholarship:* Hastings' Dictionary reports critics such as Strauss who saw the story as a simple reversal of rich and poor, with no moral contrast. https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/hdn/l/lazarus.html

**v. 26**
- Arnot: the fixed gulf is the main fact and greatest lesson of the parable: after death no one can change places. https://biblehub.com/library/arnot/the_parables_of_our_lord/xxvi_the_rich_man_and.htm
- Catholic.com: the parable teaches that one's fate is sealed at death. It also uses the story to argue for conscious existence between death and resurrection, against the Jehovah's Witness reading. https://www.catholic.com/qa/how-can-i-refute-this-watchtower-society-argument-about-the-rich-man-and-lazarus

**vv. 27–28**
- Coffman: his request is still selfish, since it concerns only his own family. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/luke-16.html

**v. 29**
- Guzik: the rich man was lost because he did not listen to the law and the prophets. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/luke/luke-16.cfm
- Preceptaustin: knowing Moses and the prophets brought greater responsibility. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-16-commentary

**v. 30**
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon: Lazarus coming back from Abraham's side would not preach better than a living preacher whose lips God has touched. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/luke/luke-16.cfm

**v. 31**
- H.B. Charles: these closing verses are the point of the parable, because how we respond to God's word has eternal results. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/charles_hb/sermons/luke/the-rich-man-and-lazarus-luke-16-v19-31.cfm
- Catholic.com: those who ignore God's word will not heed Christ's own resurrection either. https://www.catholic.com/qa/how-can-i-refute-this-watchtower-society-argument-about-the-rich-man-and-lazarus
- *Older critical scholarship:* Hastings' Dictionary reports Keim's view that John 11 turns this saying into a story, since a man did rise and the Jews still did not believe. https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/hdn/l/lazarus.html
